name: aegis (rust-aegis)
workload: AEAD encryption throughput chart at 16 KB messages (separate 64 KB chart for MAC-only)
claimed_speedup: On AMD Zen 4 (turbo disabled): AEGIS128L 208.44 Gb/s vs AES-128-GCM(BoringSSL) 50.83 Gb/s (~4.1x) and vs AES-256-GCM(BoringSSL) 47.68 Gb/s (~4.4x); AEGIS128X4 521.36 Gb/s (~10.9x vs AES-256-GCM/BoringSSL) (derived from page data)

found_via: crates.io API q=aegis, per-page=10

name: AEGIS-128X2 / AEGIS-128X4 / AEGIS-256X2 / AEGIS-256X4 (parallel AEGIS modes, libaegis)
workload: Single-core AEAD encryption throughput on 16 KB messages, comparing AEGIS-128L/256 and their X2/X4 parallel modes against OpenSSL's AES-GCM on Intel Raptor Lake (i9-13900K), AMD EPYC 7543, and AMD Ryzen 7 7700 (Zen4, VAES/AVX-512).
claimed_speedup: AEGIS-128X2: 318 Gbps vs AES128-GCM 81 Gbps on i9-13900K (~3.9x); AEGIS-128X4: 348 Gbps vs AES128-GCM 94 Gbps on Ryzen 7 7700 (~3.7x); AEGIS-256X4: 277 Gbps vs AES256-GCM 81 Gbps on Ryzen 7 7700 (~3.4x); even plain AEGIS-128L: 190 Gbps vs 81 Gbps on i9-13900K (~2.3x)
compiler_and_flags: AEGIS reference implementation in Zig (from the IETF AEGIS specification's reference code); baseline is OpenSSL 3.1.0 / 3.1.1 AES-GCM. Exact compiler/build flags for the OpenSSL side are not stated in the paper.
hardware: Intel Core i9-13900K (Raptor Lake); AMD EPYC 7543; AMD Ryzen 7 7700 (Zen4, AVX-512+VAES) — single core, 16 KB messages
stars_or_usage: 146 stars (aegis-aead/libaegis); is the reference implementation cited by the IETF AEGIS draft/RFC
tradeoffs: The X2/X4 speedups require VAES/AVX-512 or equivalent wide vector-AES instructions; on CPUs without vector-AES, plain AEGIS-128L/256 is as fast or faster than the X-variants. AEGIS has a shorter cryptanalytic track record than AES-GCM (in active study since 2013).
caveats: Benchmark is single-core and only shown for 16 KB messages in the cited tables (short-message behavior is discussed qualitatively, not tabulated here). Compiler/flags for the OpenSSL baseline build are unstated, so Tier A rests on the CPU models and public reference code being explicit. Independent corroboration: eBACS/SUPERCOP's CAESAR benchmark page shows aegis128l at ~0.24 cycles/byte vs a SUPERCOP AES-GCM reference (aes128gcmv1) at ~0.95 cycles/byte on a 2024 Intel Core 5 210H (https://bench.cr.yp.to/results-caesar/amd64-freshwrap,big.html) — that reference AES-GCM implementation is not confirmed to be OpenSSL's, so it is not used as the primary evidence here.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos aead cipher c++ (surfaced aegis-aead/libaegis); corroborated via bench.cr.yp.to/results-aead/amd64-hertz.html
IACR ePrint search q=AEGIS: https://eprint.iacr.org/2023/523 'Adding more parallelism to the AEGIS authenticated encryption algorithms'

name: hardware-rust-crypto
workload: AES-256-GCM allocation-free encrypt/decrypt (encrypt_to/decrypt_to), Criterion benchmarks over sizes 16B-16KiB
claimed_speedup: Beats ring at every size 16B-16KiB (e.g. 1.77us vs 2.38us at 16KiB encrypt: 8.64 vs 6.41 GiB/s); 14x-43x faster than an unmodified default-build RustCrypto aes-gcm 0.10, and 3.4x-5.0x faster than RustCrypto built with its ARMv8 hardware cfgs enabled
compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.96.0, cargo bench (Criterion, default release build); RustCrypto 'armv8 cfgs' variant built with RUSTFLAGS="--cfg aes_armv8 --cfg polyval_armv8"
hardware: Apple M4 Max, macOS (Darwin 25.4)
tradeoffs: AES-256-only (no AES-128), hardware-instruction-only design (no software fallback, so it hard-fails on CPUs lacking AES-NI/ARMv8 crypto extensions); extensively formally verified (Kani, SAW, crux-mir, F*, Z3) as its other main selling point besides speed
caveats: Single-run laptop benchmark; author explicitly states +/-10% run-to-run variance at sub-microsecond sizes and says to read results as 'tie/win/lose, not exact ratios' and to re-run on target Linux x86_64 hardware before integration decisions; project has only 1 GitHub star
found_via: crates.io API q=aes-ni, per-page=15

name: HiAE (High-throughput Authenticated Encryption)
workload: Single-core AEAD encrypt+authenticate throughput across 14 named ARM and x86 CPUs (server/desktop/laptop/mobile/router), message sizes 64B-16384B, -O3 builds, vs OpenSSL 3.0 AES-256-GCM, AES-256-CTR, SNOW-V-GCM, Rocca, Rocca-S and AEGIS-128L.
claimed_speedup: 16 KB AEAD: 340.02 Gbps (HiAE) vs 51.90 Gbps (AES-256-GCM) on AMD Ryzen 9 7950X (~6.5x); 171.46 Gbps vs 36.49 Gbps on Intel Xeon W9-3495X (~4.7x); 253.19 Gbps vs 38.80 Gbps on AMD EPYC 9334 (~6.5x); paper states HiAE exceeds 340 Gbps on x86 and 180 Gbps on ARM, calling it the fastest measured AEAD on ARM
compiler_and_flags: GCC 11.4 (x86 servers/desktop, Ubuntu 22.04 or WSL2), GCC 10.3 (Kunpeng/openEuler), GCC 14 (Apple M-series), ArkCompiler 3.0.0.5 (Huawei mobile), openWRT GCC 11.2.0 (router); -O3 maximum optimization used for every implementation compared
hardware: 14 named CPUs incl. Intel Xeon W9-3495X, AMD EPYC 9334, AMD Ryzen 9 7950X, Intel Xeon Gold 6326/6242R, Intel Core i7-11700, Intel Xeon E5-2620 v3, HiSilicon Kunpeng 920/920X, Kirin 9000S, Qualcomm Snapdragon 8+ Gen1, Apple M1/M2 Max/M3 Pro, Rockchip RK3568
tradeoffs: Reference repo carries no LICENSE file, so the code can be studied but not safely reused/redistributed as-is. HiAE is a brand-new (2025) design with far less cryptanalysis history than AES-GCM or even AEGIS; the paper's own results show HiAE falls slightly behind Rocca on older Xeon Gold 6242R/E5-2620 v3 CPUs that lack VAES.
caveats: Very new design (2025), under active cryptanalysis (see follow-up IACR ePrint papers 2025/1180 'Cryptanalysis of the Authenticated Stream Cipher HiAE', 2025/1203, and 2025/1235 rebutting a claimed attack). No open-source license on the reference implementation.
found_via: IACR ePrint search q=HiAE: https://eprint.iacr.org/2025/377 'HiAE: A High-Throughput Authenticated Encryption Algorithm for Cross-Platform Efficiency'

name: HiAE (libhiae)

claimed_speedup: On Apple M5 Max: HiAE 266.7 Gbps vs AES-128-GCM(OpenSSL 3.6.4) 70.8 Gbps AEAD encryption (~3.77x, derived from page data). The associated peer-reviewed-style paper (ePrint 2025/377) separately reports HiAE exceeding 340 Gbps on x86 and 180 Gbps on ARM vs OpenSSL 3.0 AES-256-GCM baseline across 14 CPUs, e.g. AMD Ryzen 9 7950X AEAD encryption 269.01 Gbps vs AES-256-GCM 84.09 Gbps (~3.2x, derived from paper Table 10)
compiler_and_flags: Apple clang 21.0.0 on macOS 26 for the M5 Max run, -O3 -march=native/-mcpu=native; the paper's x86 server results used GCC 11.4 -O3 on Ubuntu 22.04

tradeoffs: Newer, non-standardized AES-based AEAD tied to an individual IETF CFRG draft (draft-pham-cfrg-hiae) and ePrint 2025/377; best performance needs clang/zig cc rather than gcc; HiAEx2/HiAEx4 variants are explicitly experimental benchmarking-only, not part of the spec
caveats: The cleanest textual benchmark source (hiae-aead/benchmarks) has no LICENSE file of its own (unrelated to libhiae's separate MIT license); the ePrint paper is a preprint tied to an individual IETF draft, not yet published at a peer-reviewed venue
found_via: 'Known Implementations' table in hiae-aead/draft-pham-hiae README, reached from crates.io q=aes-ni search results

name: ROCCA-S
workload: AEAD encryption/decryption throughput at 64 KB messages (keystream and full AEAD with associated data + tag), measured on Apple Silicon M5 Max and AMD Ryzen 7 7700 (Zen 4)
claimed_speedup: 208.1 Gbps AEAD encryption vs OpenSSL AES-128-GCM's 70.8 Gbps at 64KB on Apple M5 Max (~2.9x, derived from page data); 174.6 Gbps encryption on Zen 4
compiler_and_flags: Apple clang 21.0.0 with -O3 -march=native (M5); clang 21.1.8 with -O3 -march=native (Zen 4); OpenSSL 3.6.4 (M5) / 3.5.5 (Zen 4)
hardware: Apple Silicon M5 Max (macOS 26); AMD Ryzen 7 7700 (Zen 4) at fixed 3.8GHz, performance governor, boost disabled
stars_or_usage: 2 stars; official reference implementation of the ESORICS 2023 paper 'An Ultra-High Throughput AES-based Authenticated Encryption Scheme for 6G'
tradeoffs: 256-bit key / 256-bit tag only; decryption is 1.5-1.9x slower than encryption at large message sizes because the AES-round-then-fold state update recovers the message block only after the AES round completes; needs AES-NI or ARM crypto extensions to hit peak throughput
caveats: The comparison numbers come from a separate repo (hiae-aead/benchmarks), maintained by the HiAE algorithm's authors rather than an independent third party, though it states full compiler/flags/CPU/OpenSSL-version methodology and ships runnable build+benchmark scripts, which is why it still qualifies for tier A. The canonical yt-nakano/rocca-s README itself only gives a standalone '>200 Gbps on i9-12900K' figure with no baseline comparison.
found_via: GitHub: search 'AEAD in:readme benchmark AES-NI' surfaced hiae-aead/benchmarks; canonical repo found via search 'rocca-s' -> yt-nakano/rocca-s

name: Rocca-S
workload: AEAD encryption/decryption throughput at 64KB messages, 4096-byte-aligned buffers, key/nonce setup included, no associated data beyond default framing
claimed_speedup: ROCCA-S AEAD encryption 208.1 Gbps vs AES-128-GCM 70.8 Gbps (~2.9x) at 64KB on Apple Silicon M5 Max (Apple clang 21.0.0, OpenSSL 3.6.4); 174.6 Gbps AEAD encryption on AMD Ryzen 7 7700 'Zen 4' (clang 21.1.8, -O3 -march=native, OpenSSL 3.5.5, AES-GCM figure not broken out for that CPU in the same table)
compiler_and_flags: Apple clang 21.0.0 (M5) / clang 21.1.8 (Zen4), -O3 -march=native (-mcpu=native on ARM)
hardware: Apple Silicon M5 Max, macOS 26; AMD Ryzen 7 7700 'Zen 4' fixed at 3.8GHz, performance governor, turbo/frequency-scaling disabled
stars_or_usage: 21 stars (jedisct1/zig-rocca-s); algorithm specified in IETF draft-nakano-rocca-s, designed for 6G by NICT/KDDI-affiliated researchers
tradeoffs: 256-bit key, 256-bit tag; decryption is up to ~1.9x slower than encryption because the message block is only recoverable after an AES round completes, unlike AEGIS; requires AES-NI/ARM crypto extensions; practical committing-attack weaknesses have been published against Rocca-S (IACR ePrint 2024/901)

name: SNOW-V-GCM
workload: Single-thread AEAD encryption throughput vs input size (64B-16384B) on a laptop CPU; SNOW-V-GCM implemented in C++ with AVX2/AES-NI/PCLMULQDQ intrinsics, benchmarked using code extracted from OpenSSL's own benchmarking harness against OpenSSL 3.0.0-dev (2019-04-01) AES-256-GCM assembly.
claimed_speedup: 16384B: 38.91 Gbps (SNOW-V-GCM) vs 34.42 Gbps (AES-256-GCM asm), ~13% faster. Advantage shrinks with message size and reverses below ~2048B (e.g. at 64B, AES-256-GCM wins: 8.54 Gbps vs 5.16 Gbps).
compiler_and_flags: Visual Studio 2017 + NASM, 'most possible optimizations switched on', native x64 build
hardware: Intel Core i7-8650U @1.90GHz (Turbo up to 4.20GHz), single thread
stars_or_usage: SNOW-V is a 3GPP/ETSI candidate stream cipher for 5G; no widely used, independently maintained open-source repo of SNOW-V-GCM was located in this search
tradeoffs: Only faster than OpenSSL AES-256-GCM for larger messages (roughly >=4KB); for short messages (<2KB) OpenSSL's hand-tuned, instruction-stitched assembly wins outright. The paper's own C++ implementation does not get GHASH "for free" the way OpenSSL's asm does.
caveats: Benchmarked on a single, now-old (2018-era) ultrabook CPU against a pre-release OpenSSL snapshot (3.0.0-dev); no maintained public repo found, so usability is 'reference' rather than 'copyable' even though full source is printed in the paper's appendix.
found_via: IACR ePrint search q=SNOW-V: https://eprint.iacr.org/2018/1143 'A new SNOW stream cipher called SNOW-V'

name: AEZ (v4)
workload: Long message (>=2048 bytes) with long associated data, AES-NI implementation (crypto_aead/aezv4/aesni), measured as cycles/byte on a real CPU via the eBACS/SUPERCOP timing harness.
claimed_speedup: ~2.7x lower cycles/byte than aes256gcmv1 (0.26 vs 0.70 median cycles/byte, long+long encrypt) (derived from page data)
hardware: amd64, Raptor Cove P-cores, 2024 Intel Core 5 210H, 4 x 2200MHz (eBACS machine "freshwrap,big")
stars_or_usage: 104 stars (floodyberry/supercop mirror); still included in current eBACS/SUPERCOP releases

caveats: Public-domain dedication (Ted Krovetz, 'free and unencumbered software'), so 'no patent grant' applies. Baseline is SUPERCOP's own aes256gcmv1, not literally OpenSSL. Mirror is a stale 2016 snapshot; numbers are read from the live bench.cr.yp.to page (supercop-20260627 dataset). Compiler not stated on this results page, capping tier at B.
found_via: GitHub: gh search code "AEZ" "authenticated encryption" -> floodyberry/supercop:crypto_aead/aezv4; cross-checked against eBACS AEAD results page

name: Bitsliced AEGIS-128L / AEGIS-128X2 (constant-time, no-AES-NI platforms)
workload: Single-core, 16 KB message AEAD encrypt+authenticate throughput on ARM/RISC-V CPUs lacking AES instructions and on WebAssembly, plus ARM Cortex-M4 cycle counts, vs side-channel-protected (bitsliced) AES-128-GCM from OpenSSL 3.3 (on Cortex-A53) and BoringSSL (elsewhere); also a pure-TypeScript benchmark on Apple M5 Max/Bun vs the noble-ciphers pure-JS AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305.
claimed_speedup: ARM Cortex-A53: 423 Mb/s (AEGIS-128L) vs 261 Mb/s (protected AES-GCM), ~1.6x; WebAssembly on Apple M1 host: 2912 Mb/s (AEGIS-128X2) vs 480 Mb/s (protected AES-GCM), ~6.1x; SpacemiT X60 RISC-V: 333 Mb/s vs 137 Mb/s, ~2.4x; Cortex-M4: 185 cycles/byte (bitsliced AEGIS-128L) vs 246 c/B protected / 208 c/B unprotected AES-128-GCM; pure-JS on Apple M5 Max at 1 MB: 324 MB/s (AEGIS-128L) vs 182 MB/s (AES-128-GCM, ~1.8x) and 256 MB/s (ChaCha20-Poly1305, ~1.3x)
hardware: ARM Cortex-A53 (64-bit); SpacemiT X60 (RISC-V, no AES ext.); SiFive U74 (RISC-V, no AES ext.); WebAssembly on an Apple M1 host; ARM Cortex-M4 microcontroller; Apple M5 Max (pure TypeScript under Bun)
stars_or_usage: 9 stars (aegis-aead/aegis-bitsliced); companion pure-TypeScript port jedisct1/js-aegis-aead (MIT, 4 stars) used for the JS numbers
tradeoffs: Purpose-built for platforms lacking AES/vector-AES instructions (microcontrollers, RISC-V without crypto extensions, WASM, plain JS). On hardware with AES-NI/VAES, hardware-accelerated AEGIS or the AEGIS-X modes (see separate entry) are faster than this bitsliced code.
caveats: Published 2026-09, very recent and not yet independently reproduced outside the authors' own two repos. The paper states baselines were 'built and run on the same machines' but does not spell out exact compiler/flags for those builds, so this is capped at Tier B rather than A despite naming every CPU and publishing all code.
found_via: IACR ePrint search q=AEGIS: https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1338 'Bitslicing the AEGIS'

name: LeMac
baseline: GHASH (the universal-hash MAC component of OpenSSL AES-GCM)
workload: Universal-hash/MAC throughput per 128-bit message block, 2 AES-round calls per block
claimed_speedup: 0.068 cycles/byte on Intel Ice Lake, described by the authors as a 60% throughput improvement over the state-of-the-art AES-based universal hash function (abstract does not name GHASH specifically or give its own cycles/byte)
hardware: Intel Ice Lake (exact CPU model, RAM and compiler not stated in the abstract)
stars_or_usage: 2 stars (reference implementation repo); algorithm published IACR Trans. Symmetric Cryptol. (ToSC) 2024/2
tradeoffs: LeMac is a MAC/universal-hash primitive, not a complete AEAD; it must be paired with a stream cipher (e.g. AES-CTR) to form a full AES-GCM replacement, so it cannot be dropped in on its own; a sibling construction (LeMac-0) had a message-schedule bug in the original paper, fixed in this repo; CC0-1.0 dedication carries no patent grant
caveats: The abstract's speedup is versus an unnamed 'state-of-the-art' AES-based universal hash function, not an explicitly named comparison to OpenSSL's GHASH; no compiler, exact CPU model, or flags are given, so this is capped at Tier B with reduced confidence; the companion benchmark suite in the same repo (which also builds GCM, Rocca, Rocca-S, HiAE, AEGIS and Tiaoxin from source) ships no pre-generated results, only a script to run locally
found_via: SUPERCOP eBACS AEAD benchmark fastest implementations -> found via 'Rocca: reference code from the ePrint paper' cross-reference inside AugustinBariant/Implementations_LeMac_PetitMac benchmark README -> IACR ToSC article 11619

name: Rocca
workload: AEAD encryption throughput (Gbps) over inputs of 64-16384 bytes with 13 bytes of associated data, benchmarked against OpenSSL 3.1.0-dev's AES-256-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 plus SNOW-V-GCM, AEGIS-128/128L/256 and Tiaoxin-346
claimed_speedup: 150.95 Gbps (Rocca AEAD) vs 29.08 Gbps AES-256-GCM (~5.2x) and 7.60 Gbps ChaCha20-Poly1305 (~19.9x) at 16384 bytes on Intel Core i7-1068NG7 (paper Table 7); up to 235.45 Gbps vs 44.82 Gbps AES-256-GCM (~5.3x, derived from page data) on i9-12900K (paper Appendix Table 8)
hardware: Intel Core i7-1068NG7 @ 2.30GHz, 32GB RAM (primary Table 7); also i9-12900K, i9-11900, i9-10910 in Appendix A
stars_or_usage: 5 stars (ericlagergren/rocca implementation); algorithm published in IACR Trans. Symmetric Cryptol. (ToSC) 2022/1, extended from FSE 2021
tradeoffs: 256-bit key, 128-bit tag; needs AES-NI+SSE3 (x86) or Crypto+NEON (ARMv8) to hit these speeds, falls back slow otherwise; far less cryptanalysis than AES-GCM/ChaCha20-Poly1305; no nonce-misuse resistance; the closely related Rocca-S variant has since had practical committing-attack weaknesses published
caveats: The benchmark is run by the algorithm's own authors (paper Table 7/Appendix A), not an independent third party, though it directly measures OpenSSL's own AES-256-GCM/ChaCha20-Poly1305 implementations rather than reference numbers from elsewhere; exact compiler and optimization flags are not stated (only that _mm_aesenc_si128/_mm_xor_si128 intrinsics were used), which caps the tier at B; the ericlagergren/rocca repo is an independent, unofficial C/ASM port that has been dormant since early 2022
found_via: SUPERCOP eBACS AEAD benchmark fastest implementations -> gh search code 'Rocca aesenc' -> IACR ePrint 2022/116 (Rocca: An Efficient AES-based Encryption Scheme for Beyond 5G) Table 7 and Appendix A

name: Rocca (AES-based AEAD for 6G, original/pre-attack version)
workload: Single-thread AEAD encryption throughput at message sizes 64B-16384B on an Intel Core i7-1068NG7, benchmarked against OpenSSL 3.1.0-dev's AES-256-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305, plus SNOW-V-GCM and SUPERCOP implementations of AEGIS/Tiaoxin-346.
claimed_speedup: 16384B AEAD: Rocca 150.95 Gbps vs AES-256-GCM 29.08 Gbps (~5.2x) and vs ChaCha20-Poly1305 7.60 Gbps (~19.9x); also stated as 4.16x faster than SNOW-V and 3.10x faster than AES-256-CTR in encryption-only mode
hardware: Intel Core i7-1068NG7 @2.30GHz, 32GB RAM (appendix also reports an Intel Core i9-12900K)
stars_or_usage: Published at a peer-reviewed venue (IACR ePrint 2022/116 / ToSC-adjacent); no widely used reference repo for the original Rocca was located
tradeoffs: The original Rocca was later shown to have practical forgery/committing weaknesses (see IACR ePrint 2024/901 and the ToSC 2024/2025 Derbez et al. and Takeuchi et al. papers) and was superseded by the redesigned Rocca-S. Treat these numbers as a data point on the AES-NI+SIMD 'wide round function' technique, not as a currently-recommended cipher.
caveats: This entry covers the ORIGINAL Rocca design, now considered broken/superseded by Rocca-S; compiler/flags for the OpenSSL comparison are not stated in the paper (hardware is), which caps this at Tier B; no maintained open-source repo of the original Rocca was found in this session (a separate, unrelated Rocca-S implementation exists at jedisct1/zig-rocca-s but was not benchmarked against a named baseline in that repo, so it is not reported as its own entry here).

name: tape-sha256
baseline: sha2 crate (serial SHA-256); also OpenSSL SHA-256 via Node.js node:crypto, and C batch hashers Firedancer fd_sha256 and isa-l_crypto sha256_mb
workload: Batch of 64 independent messages (26-byte prefix plus about 1 KiB payload, 67,680 bytes per batch, one Solana erasure batch of Merkle leaves), one thread pinned to one core, best of 15 rounds of 50 iterations; also hash chains in ns per link and Merkle commitments.
claimed_speedup: BENCHMARKS.md summary vs sha2: AMD Zen 5 3.5x (avx512-2x16), Zen 4 2.1x (shani-x4), Zen 3 2.1x, Intel Emerald / Granite Rapids 2.0-2.1x, Apple M-series 6.8x; Zen 5 7.82 us/batch (8654 MB/s) vs sha2 27.71 us (2443 MB/s). Versus C implementations: 60% faster than Firedancer and 39% faster than the best isa-l_crypto result on Zen 5, about 8% faster than Firedancer on Zen 4, about 2.2x on Zen 3, but 2-12% slower than Firedancer on Intel Emerald Rapids / Granite Rapids in measured runs. Hash chains: 7.3 ns/link at 32 chains vs sha2 45.4 ns on Zen 5 (6.0x). OpenSSL: benches/wasm/README.md says the native neon-sha2-x4 batch (about 16 us; BENCHMARKS.md lists 16.25 us) is 2.7x faster than node:crypto (OpenSSL), whose crypto.hash one-shot took 42.89 us/batch (1578 MB/s) on an M4 Max (unpinned, read as ratios).
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.89+ (rust-version) cargo bench, release profile; RUSTFLAGS not stated for native rows (notes that -C target-cpu=native made the Zen 5 interlaced kernel 8-14% slower); wasm rows built with -C target-feature=+simd128; Firedancer and isa-l_crypto built from source with unstated flags
hardware: AMD Zen 5 (family 0x1a, model not captured, 2026-08-08); EPYC 9B14 (GCP c3d); EPYC 7B13 (GCP c2d); Xeon Platinum 8581C (GCP c4); Xeon 6985P-C (GCP c4-standard-8-lssd); Apple M-series (M4 Max per the wasm README)
stars_or_usage: crates.io: 470 downloads, versions 0.1.0 (2026-07-27) and 0.2.1 (2026-08-11); GitHub repo returns 404
tradeoffs: Pure Rust (stable, no C dependency) multi-buffer SHA-256: hash_many, hash_many_prefixed, hash_pairs for independent messages (SIMD lane per message) and hash_chain / hash_chains for iterated 32-byte hashing (Solana proof-of-history). Runtime dispatch over AVX-512, AVX2, SHA-NI, ARM SHA-2, NEON, WebAssembly simd128 and portable fallbacks. No streaming single-message API, so a single large message gets no speedup; pre-1.0. WebCrypto beats the wasm build for batched ~1 KB messages in Chrome.
caveats: The GitHub repository named in the crates.io repository field (https://github.com/spool-labs/tape-sha256) returns HTTP 404, so it is private or removed; code, benches and BENCHMARKS.md were read from the crates.io 0.2.1 tarball (last_commit unknown: .cargo_vcs_info.json records git sha 5e72f679f750fe9e7fe166ae832003739e868e14). First-party measurements by the author, and the main baseline is the Rust sha2 crate, not OpenSSL; the only OpenSSL comparison is through Node.js (call overhead included, M4 Max unpinned, native batch number from a different document than the node:crypto number, so cross-run). Benchmarks are same-machine paired but compiler flags and several CPU models (Zen 5, Apple) are not captured. Does not win everywhere: 2-12% slower than Firedancer on Intel Emerald / Granite Rapids; the Firedancer harness builds prefix||leaf outside the timed region while tape reads prefix and body from separate slices. Results are single-core batch hashing, not application speedups (the README also cites 14-21% faster Agave shred recovery, unverified). Tests cross-check every backend against the sha2 crate.

name: Rain (Rainbow hash)
baseline: HighwayHash-128 and FarmHash-128.CM (128-bit hashes in the SMHasher3 results table); the repo names no baseline itself
workload: SMHasher3 Speed test as published in the SMHasher3 results README: average cycles/hash over 1-31-byte keys and bulk bytes/cycle at 262144-byte keys, Rainbow 128-bit and 256-bit v3.7.1 against the other hashes that pass all tests. Results page does not name the CPU (harness prints '@ 3.5 ghz').
claimed_speedup: Claim only (README): 'Rainbow is the fastest 128-bit hash, and the fastest 256-bit hash (non-crypto)'; README table gives Rainbow 3-6 GiB/s with no baseline. SMHasher3 results page data: rainbow-128 62.06 cycles on 1-31 byte keys vs HighwayHash-128 99.09 (~1.6x faster, derived from page data), FarmHash-128.CM.seed1 69.61 (~1.1x), MeowHash 61.51 (tie); rainbow-256 103.65 vs HighwayHash-256 154.48 (~1.5x) and PearsonBlock-256 168.68. Not faster elsewhere: rainbow-128 is slower than a5hash-128 (30.27) and MuseAir-128 (30.97) on short keys, and bulk is 1.27 bytes/cycle (4.14 GiB/s at the assumed 3.5 GHz) vs HighwayHash-128 2.87, a5hash-128 6.92, MuseAir-128 7.15 and MeowHash 12.43; rainbow-256 bulk 1.28 vs HighwayHash-256 2.88 and RH512 2.50.
tradeoffs: Rainbow is a roughly 140-line multiply/rotate hash with scalable 64, 128 or 256-bit output that passes all 250 SMHasher3 tests (64-bit variant claimed), but its bulk speed is low (about 1.3 bytes/cycle). The repo also ships Rainstorm, a slower experimental crypto-style hash whose v4 README says an external review found a practical collision for a two-message-round reduction; it is unvetted. WASM port is 4x to 23x slower than the C++ build (README benchmark).
caveats: The README headline claim (fastest 128-bit and 256-bit non-crypto hash) is not supported by the SMHasher3 results page it links: several passing 128-bit hashes (a5hash-128, MuseAir-128, MeowHash) are faster in bulk and on short keys, and at 256 bits HighwayHash-256 and CityHashCrc-256 (which fails some tests) are faster in bulk. The only wins found are narrow (short-key latency against HighwayHash and FarmHash). SMHasher3 results list the CPU nowhere and the table is the maintainer's single run; Rain's README credits SMHasher3's maintainer for improvements to the code, so the suite is not fully arm's length. The claim may predate v3.7.1 (not checked). The repo's own results/smhasher3/rainbow-256-v3.7.1.txt came back as an empty file through raw.githubusercontent.com and was not used. The assigned URL github.com/DOSAYGO-Research/rain resolves to DOSAYGO-STUDIO/rain.
